stories.topic: The Girl Who Learned To Write On Her Mother's Gravestone
stories.summary: On a cold winter afternoon in London, a man takes his young daughter to St. Pancras churchyard, to the grave of her mother. The girl sits by the gravestone and traces the letters inscribed there with a tiny finger — that is how she learns to write. The mother died of childbed fever days after giving birth; the daughter would carry guilt for her birth having killed her mother. Both, as it happens, would write books that changed the world: Mary Wollstonecraft and Mary Shelley.
stories.insight: The frame of the episode in a single image. Outlaws don't appear from nowhere — they often inherit the burden, the books, and the bereavement of an earlier outlaw. Progress is dynastic before it is institutional.

stories.topic: Mary Wollstonecraft Walks Up And Down In The Rain Before Jumping Into The Thames
stories.summary: After her lover proves unfaithful, Wollstonecraft decides to drown herself in the Thames. It is raining. She walks up and down the embankment for half an hour before jumping — deliberately, so her clothes get heavy and she will be more likely to sink. She writes a suicide letter to her lover saying she has chosen the Thames because no one who goes in there comes out alive. A bystander pulls her out anyway.
stories.insight: The intellectual outlaw isn't shielded from despair — she is more exposed to it. The same precision of mind that produced A Vindication of the Rights of Woman is at work in the calculation about the rain-soaked dress. Pioneering and pain are often the same faculty turned in different directions.

stories.topic: Wollstonecraft Frames Women's Equality In The Only Language That Could Be Heard
stories.summary: In A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Wollstonecraft argues that if men would 'snap our chains and be content with rational fellowship in instead of slavish obedience, they would find us more observant daughters, more affectionate sisters, more faithful wives, more reasonable mothers, in a word, better citizens.' Amit notes the tragic constraint: she has to argue not 'we will be autonomous and live fulfilling lives without you,' but 'this is what we will be to you' — because her only readers are men who read political philosophy.
stories.insight: The first generation of any radical idea has to be smuggled inside the assumptions of its enemies. The radicalism is real, but it has to wear the costume of the audience to get through the door. Read the constraint, not just the text.

stories.topic: Mary Shelley Invents Science Fiction At Eighteen With No Models
stories.summary: On Lake Geneva in 1816, eighteen-year-old Mary Shelley sits with Percy Shelley, Byron, and Polidori around a fire trading ideas for stories. Polidori has heard the anatomist William Lawrence argue there is no soul — consciousness is just organs. Mary Shelley, raised on Milton's Paradise Lost, hears its line ('Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay / To mould Me man?') and writes Frankenstein — a Chinese-box of three nested narrators (captain, Frankenstein, monster) at a time when fiction is told by an omniscient narrator. There is no genre called science fiction. Brian Aldiss would later call it the first.
stories.insight: When you write the first work in a genre, every move you make is later mistaken for cliche. The sexist reaction was 'her husband must have written it' — in fact Percy Shelley contributed about 4,000 of 78,000 words, and they read worse. Sui generis work has to be defended twice: against its rejecters and, later, against its imitators.

stories.topic: Ignaz Semmelweis Solves Childbed Fever — And Is Beaten To Death In An Asylum For It
stories.summary: At Vienna General Hospital in 1846, Semmelweis notices Ward One has a 10% maternal mortality rate while Ward Two has 4%. After much process-of-elimination he traces it to doctors going from washing corpses straight into delivering babies. He institutes chlorinated handwashing and the rate drops to zero in two years. But germ theory does not yet exist; he cannot explain why it works. He is offended-against by colleagues for the social-class implication that doctors are unclean, sacked from his post, and dies in 1865 in a Viennese asylum from a gangrenous arm caused by a beating from the wardens.
stories.insight: Solving the problem isn't enough. Without a mechanism, the establishment will not accept the result — and being right while seeming socially offensive is the worst possible combination. The episode of medicine that was 'wash your hands' took decades because washing hands implied doctors had been killing women.

stories.topic: The Suicidal Doctor Who Believed Semmelweis
stories.summary: Somewhere in the chain of correspondence Semmelweis tries to start, one physician actually believes him. The physician then realises he had recently attended a delivery without washing his hands, and the woman — a relative — died. He kills himself.
stories.insight: The moral cost of being right late. Belief in a true theory is not always a gift; for the convert, it can be a discovery of guilt for past acts done in good faith. Outlaw ideas wound their first followers as much as their last opponents.

stories.topic: Alfred Wegener Stares At A Map Until Continents Move
stories.summary: Wegener, a German meteorologist, looks at the eastern coast of South America and the western coast of Africa and notices they fit like jigsaw pieces. He proposes in 1912 that they were once joined and have since drifted apart, predicting matching fossils and rock formations on either side — and finds them. But he has no mechanism for what 'mighty force' moves continents. Geologists deride him. He dies on a Greenland expedition in 1930. Plate tectonics is finally accepted in the 1960s — Ajay remembers, as a child, his father excited about this 'new' science.
stories.insight: Pattern recognition is not enough; the world wants the gear-train. A theory that predicts well but cannot say how is forced into a generation-long waiting room. The map was open in front of everyone — only one person actually looked.

stories.topic: Boltzmann Hangs Himself Two Years Before Vindication
stories.summary: In the 1860s-70s Boltzmann pioneered statistical mechanics — bringing probability through and through into physics, linking microscopic states of atoms to macroscopic temperature and entropy. The catch: microscopes weren't yet good enough to see atoms at all. Critics asked: 'Have you ever seen one?' He couldn't get jobs, was hounded out of Vienna, and committed suicide in 1906 — only a couple of years before atomic theory was vindicated and his framework became central. His tombstone in Vienna carries his equation: S = k log W.
stories.insight: Timing is the cruellest variable. Being right by two years too early, in a career that runs for decades, is functionally identical to being wrong. The distance between asylum and Nobel is sometimes a single funeral.

stories.topic: Darwin Plods For Twenty-Two Years; Wallace Cracks It With Malaria
stories.summary: Darwin had the theory of evolution in 1837, a year after the Beagle. He understood instantly that publishing it would be a 'personal disaster' — beheading-level — so he spent twenty-two years writing and revising. Meanwhile in the jungles of Indonesia, Alfred Russel Wallace, in a 106-degree malarial fever, cracked the same theory from scratch and came home ready to present at the Royal Society. Friends who knew Darwin's secret organised a simultaneous joint presentation in 1859. Both still lacked the missing piece: mechanism. That came when Mendel's quietly self-printed run of forty plant-genetics pamphlets was finally connected to evolution decades later — and biology got its first real theory.
stories.insight: Two failure modes coexist in pioneers — Darwin's careful twenty-two-year fortification, Wallace's bias-for-action. Caution risks being scooped; speed risks being ignored. A discipline becomes itself only when several stalled outlaw insights are finally welded together by a later generation.

stories.summary: Gregor Mendel, an obscure monk in Austria, derived the laws of inheritance from pea plants — one of the most important moments in the history of science. He printed forty copies of his paper, because that was all he could afford. He sent some out. A few people got it; most filed it as 'cute, we already breed plants.' His magnificence was not understood for decades.
stories.insight: The physical economics of communication used to gate the diffusion of ideas. Mendelian genetics existed for a generation as forty photocopies in forty drawers. The world was not too stupid for the truth — the printing press was too expensive.

stories.topic: John Snow, W.C. Pernell, And The Caste Map Of Cholera
stories.summary: John Snow worked out in mid-19th-century London that cholera was waterborne; the resistance, especially in India, took decades. Late in the century, W.C. Pernell drew a cholera map of an Indian village and noticed something striking: most of the dead were of higher caste. The reason — they drank from a well that had become contaminated, and the lower castes were forbidden to use it. The only low-caste victim was a washerman who washed the upper-caste clothes.
stories.insight: Epidemiology can become a satire of social structure. A truth about water turned out to also be a truth about caste; a truth about access turned out to also be a truth about exclusion. The data didn't care about the social order — it indicted it.

stories.topic: Kati Kariko's Years Of 'No, No, No'
stories.summary: Long before mRNA vaccines saved much of the planet during the COVID pandemic, Katalin Kariko spent years grinding on mRNA research. She has said that every night she would work on grant applications — 'grant, grant, grant' — and every reply came back 'no, no, no.' She was treated as a fringe researcher for decades.
stories.insight: We canonise the survivors. For every Kariko there are unknown Karikos who quit, retired, died, or never got the grant — whose theories may have been just as right. The lesson isn't that perseverance pays; it's that survivorship bias makes perseverance look more reliable than it is.

stories.topic: Keynes's Heart Attack Under The Staircase
stories.summary: On a recent visit to Washington DC, Ajay was driven around by Vikram Raghavan — a World Bank lawyer for whom history is 'his whole life.' Raghavan stopped at a particular building, pointed under a staircase, and said: this is where John Maynard Keynes had a heart attack. Ajay wondered if Keynes, recovering, had quipped 'in the long run we are all dead' — but in fact Keynes survived that one.
stories.insight: A small set-piece in praise of monomaniacal friendships. The historian-friend doesn't merely know dates; they overlay every street with a layer the rest of us cannot see. To walk a city with such a person is to be temporarily upgraded into a richer reality.

stories.topic: Population Column Backlash As Aggressive-Conventional In Action
stories.summary: When Amit wrote a column arguing that population is not a problem but a strength, readers reflexively got angry — not with his argument but with him. Instead of engaging, they 'gali nala gay.' He realised they were taught in school that population is the problem; he had attacked a tile in their identity-package, and they reacted as if attacked.
stories.insight: Aggressive conventionality is identity-defense costumed as argument. Once a belief gets fused with the self, attacking the belief becomes attacking the self — which is why the response is rage, not refutation. The way to spot the difference: if the rebuttal is to your argument or to you.

recommendations.creator: Charlotte Gordon
recommendations.context: Dual biography of Mary Wollstonecraft and Mary Shelley — source of much of the dope for the first two chapters.
recommendations.reason: Tells the mother-and-daughter saga as one continuous story of two lives lived against the grain. Gordon's prose furnishes the chilling description of the legal status of women in Wollstonecraft's England — a world where chimpanzees got legal protection in 1824, twenty years before the first law that limited (but did not prohibit) wife-beating.

recommendations.item: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
recommendations.creator: Mary Wollstonecraft
recommendations.context: The 1792 founding text of feminist philosophy, written when there were no role models for the argument.
recommendations.reason: Today its arguments can read tame; modern feminists may find it hedged. Read as written — for an audience of male political philosophers in a world where wives could not own property — and the radicalism is unmistakable. Wollstonecraft also derives virtue from reason rather than religion or tradition, an attack on a much wider set of structures than gender.

recommendations.creator: Mary Shelley
recommendations.context: The first work of science fiction, written by an eighteen-year-old in 1816-18 with no models for the genre.
recommendations.reason: Read for the structure as much as the story — three nested first-person narrators (captain, Frankenstein, monster) where the convention of the day was an omniscient voice. Read also as the live AI-ethics question of 1818: if we create a being with consciousness, what do we owe it? Modern science fiction tackles the biggest questions of the present, and Shelley invented that move.

recommendations.item: The Vindication of the Rights of Woman (Episode 2, The Book Club)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's fifteen-minute Storytel episode on Wollstonecraft's book.
recommendations.reason: A quick on-ramp into the argument and the world it was made in.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's Storytel episode on Mary Shelley's novel.
recommendations.reason: Companion piece to the Wollstonecraft episode — designed to be heard back-to-back like the mother-daughter story.

recommendations.creator: John Milton
recommendations.context: The epic poem whose lines about Adam asking the Maker 'did I request thee, Maker, from my clay / to mould me man?' inspired Mary Shelley.
recommendations.reason: The germ of Frankenstein's moral question — the creature confronting its creator — is already in Milton. A reminder that no work is truly sui generis: even the inventor of a genre is rewriting the books she grew up with.

recommendations.creator: Denis Villeneuve
recommendations.context: A meditation on memory and the shaping of the self, in the Frankenstein lineage.
recommendations.reason: Amit's example of science fiction at the level of literature — biggest questions of modern times, treated seriously, in a form mistaken for genre.

recommendations.creator: Alex Garland
recommendations.context: Garland's film about a created intelligence and its rights.
recommendations.reason: Same Frankenstein-question in a new register: if we create something that approaches consciousness, what does it owe us — and we it?

recommendations.creator: Sherwin Nuland
recommendations.context: Nuland's book-length account of Ignaz Semmelweis and the discovery of handwashing.
recommendations.reason: The fullest narrative of the Semmelweis tragedy — solved problem, no mechanism, social-class offence, asylum, gangrene. The cost of being right too early, told in detail.

recommendations.item: Are You Just One Version of Yourself? (Episode 3, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Earlier EIE episode on contingent character and how small things change who we become.
recommendations.reason: Referenced in the discussion of Semmelweis's late-life mental decline — a way to think about whether his character changed because of how the world treated him, or independently of it.

recommendations.creator: Jacob Bronowski
recommendations.context: Bronowski's book and BBC TV series tracing the history of scientific and intellectual progress.
recommendations.reason: The source of much of Ajay's stock of stories about intellectual outlaws — Wegener, Boltzmann, Darwin, Mendel. Watched as a child, never lost. The kind of work that programs in admiration for the maverick before the world has had a chance to teach you to fear them.

recommendations.item: Newton the Alchemist. Gandhi the Black Swan (Episode 7, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Earlier EIE episode taking great figures off their pedestals.
recommendations.reason: Sets up the point Ajay returns to here: a WikiLeaks dump from any free thinker's life would contain rubbish, and that's the point. Free thinking and impropriety often come bundled.

recommendations.creator: Chinmay Tumbe
recommendations.context: Tumbe's book on the history of pandemics, including John Snow, W.C. Pernell, and the caste map of cholera in India.
recommendations.reason: Tells the parallel cholera story to Semmelweis's puerperal fever — including Pernell's caste-stratified cholera map of an Indian village, where the only low-caste victim was the washerman who handled upper-caste clothes.

recommendations.creator: Paul Graham
recommendations.context: Graham's essay splitting people on two axes (independent vs conventional, passive vs aggressive) and naming each quadrant's characteristic call.
recommendations.reason: The frame the episode uses to make sense of why outlaws get persecuted. The aggressively conventional-minded — common, loud, status-seeking within tribes — are not the silly herd but the active enforcers of convention. Graham's Princeton-professor anecdote (white Southerners pre-abolition) is also cited: hindsight admiration for outlaws is cheap; we are not noticing today's outlaws either.

recommendations.item: Population Is Not a Problem, but Our Greatest Strength
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column arguing against the Malthusian framing of India's population.
recommendations.reason: Cited as a personal experience of the aggressively-conventional reaction in the wild: readers angry not at the argument but at the fact of disagreement, because the 'population is a problem' belief had become tile in their identity.

recommendations.item: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode developing the population argument.
recommendations.reason: The longer treatment of why people are brains, not stomachs — and why the 'population problem' is always a governance failure in disguise.

recommendations.item: Who's Got the Guts to Go to the Moon?
recommendations.creator: Adam Mastroianni
recommendations.context: Mastroianni's essay arguing that modern research is structurally too safe — no moonshots.
recommendations.reason: Provides the three-step pattern for outlaw ideas: '1. A weirdo outsider proposes some new idea. 2. Experts and authorities ignore or suppress it because it seems stupid. This can go on for a long time. 3. Eventually, the new idea wins out because it is a good idea.' And it argues the modern system is so disincentive-loaded that step 1 barely happens any more.

recommendations.creator: Tyler Cowen / Mercatus Center
recommendations.context: A grants programme funding mad ideas from non-credentialed people; Shruti Rajagopalan runs the India branch.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's pointer to the institutional answer to Mastroianni's diagnosis — fund the weirdos directly, bypassing the credentialed conventional pipeline.

recommendations.item: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Earlier EIE episode on what's broken in the world of knowledge production.
recommendations.reason: The longer treatment of Ajay's argument here — that the institutional ladder (school, college, PhD, papers, grants, tenure) selects systematically against the creative weirdos who actually drive progress. The conscientiousness trait gets selected for; the others get winnowed away.

recommendations.item: The Story of My Experiments with Truth
recommendations.creator: Mohandas Gandhi
recommendations.context: Gandhi's autobiography, in which he documents his own oddballness in detail.
recommendations.reason: Most outlaws don't write a book like this — but Gandhi did, voluntarily exposing his own peculiarity. Read against modern surveillance culture, it is a model for what we'd find about any free thinker if we cared to look — and a warning that the 'sugar-coated' versions of Newton or Solzhenitsyn we admire today wouldn't survive a WikiLeaks dump of their lives.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Education (Episode 54, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Earlier EIE episode on education.
recommendations.reason: Companion to the chapter on selection bias in academic and intellectual careers — how each rung filters for conformity.

recommendations.creator: Ludwig Boltzmann
recommendations.context: His grave carries the inscription S = k log W — his own equation for entropy.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's 'oddball' recommendation of the episode: visit it. The tombstone vindicates a man who hanged himself in 1906 and was proven right within years — a physical monument to the cost and the eventual victory of the scientific outlaw.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Standard EIE reference for Ajay's work on policy, including the analysis of why critics are systematically undersupplied.
recommendations.reason: Returning reference behind Ajay's running framing of the lone dissenter's economics — positive externality, private cost.

core_ideas.explanation: Progress happens slowly. In every age, a small number of people are intellectually ahead of their time — thinking things that will later be considered normal, but at the time are radical. They are shunned, despised, sacked, ridiculed, or driven to suicide; they are vindicated decades later, often after their deaths. The episode strings together a relay-race of such lives — Wollstonecraft, Shelley, Semmelweis, Wegener, Boltzmann, Darwin, Wallace, Mendel, Snow, Pernell, Kariko — to show this isn't a series of unfortunate accidents but a recurring pattern in how knowledge moves.
core_ideas.quote: And we came up with a bunch of those stories.

core_ideas.explanation: A new theory can predict accurately and still be rejected if it cannot say HOW the predicted thing happens. Semmelweis demonstrated that handwashing eliminated childbed fever but had no germ theory — so 'where is the mechanism?' was the killer question. Wegener showed continents fit and shared fossils but had no force to move them — same killer question. Darwin showed evolution acted but couldn't supply the genetic mechanism (Mendel's work was sitting unread). Boltzmann's statistical mechanics worked predictively, but no microscope yet showed an atom. The mechanism gap is the most reliable cause of generation-long delays.

Paul Graham's frame: people split on two axes — conventional vs independent thinking, and passive vs aggressive enforcement — into four quadrants. The most common is passively conventional-minded ('what will the neighbours think?'). The second most common is aggressively conventional-minded ('crush outgroup!'). The least common is the aggressively independent-minded ('eppur si muove'). Graham argues — and Amit and Ajay agree — that the aggressively conventional-minded are the greatest danger to progress, because they enforce received wisdom they have not actually thought about.
core_ideas.quote: The greatest danger to progress is from the aggressively conventional-minded.

core_ideas.concept: Why The Aggressively Conventional Are Aggressive
core_ideas.explanation: The episode poses this as the central puzzle. Ajay's answer: they are upholding a system. There is a whole establishment with organisations, credentials, journals, jobs, funding, tenure — and a tacit game of upholding it. Aggressive conventionality is bureaucratic self-defence in cognitive form. Amit's complementary answer: when a belief becomes fused with identity (taught in school, repeated by tribe), an attack on the belief is experienced as an attack on the self, so the response is rage rather than refutation.
core_ideas.quote: It is the same as any other bureaucracy. What bureaucracies want is to keep the boat steady.

core_ideas.concept: The Survivorship Bias of Outlaw Stories
core_ideas.explanation: We remember Semmelweis, Wegener, Boltzmann, and Kariko because they were eventually validated — even if posthumously. But for every one of them, there are a hundred others who were equally right and were never vindicated, who died unknown, whose pamphlets sit unread, whose grants kept getting rejected until they quit. Our admiration is shaped by the survivors. The lesson is not 'persistence is rewarded'; it is 'most outlaws lose, and we don't even know their names.'
core_ideas.quote: There's a survivor bias here. We remember these people because these people are the ones who made it out.

core_ideas.explanation: Robert George of Princeton asks his history students: imagine you are a white person living in the deep South before abolition. Are you going to be an abolitionist? Every hand goes up. The fact is almost no one would have been. We admire today's vindicated outlaws because they have already been certified by the present; the test is whether we can recognise today's outlaws when they look like cranks. Almost certainly we are failing it on someone right now.
core_ideas.quote: There are Darwins and Mendels around us who we probably ignore and we think of them as weird and we're not taking them seriously.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's framing: the conformist filters most of us run — clean shirt, right speech, laughs at the right jokes, one of the gang — are screening out the very people most likely to have creative new ideas, because there's a causal connection between being a non-conformist weirdo and having genuine imagination. So upgrading our personal filters to take oddballs seriously is a self-interested arbitrage, not just a moral duty. It's a literal undervalued asset class — pay attention now, before the world catches up.
core_ideas.quote: These are five hundred dollar bills lying on the ground.

core_ideas.concept: Conscientiousness Is The Only Trait Selected For
core_ideas.explanation: Of the Big Five personality traits, the modern intellectual ladder — school exams, college grades, PhD, journal papers, grants, tenure — selects almost exclusively for conscientiousness. The other traits (openness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism — and creativity, which lives partly in openness) are not just unselected but actively winnowed away, because reaching the top requires playing the game, dressing right, laughing at the right jokes, not rocking boats. The result is a stable, well-funded, credentialed establishment systematically depleted of the creative weirdos who could make it produce real progress.
core_ideas.quote: We are systematically winnowing away the creative people, the mavericks, the free thinkers, the people with the nerve to challenge the establishment.

core_ideas.explanation: There is probably a causal connection between imagination and weirdness. To have the level of dreaming of a Boltzmann, you are probably not a well-adjusted, well-socialised person — because if you had been, you would have been more vulnerable to social programming and would have absorbed your elders' messages. The very faculty of creative invention requires some failure of conventional socialisation. Many oddballs are not creative thinkers, but a disproportionate number of creative thinkers are oddballs — and society's machinery of polite acceptance rejects them as a class.
core_ideas.quote: The very act of imagination, the very act of creativity is probably grounded in being a bit of a weirdo.

core_ideas.explanation: We today admire sugar-coated versions of Newton, Sakharov, Solzhenitsyn, Gandhi — only the highlights of their journeys. If a WikiLeaks dump appeared from any of their lives, it would contain all kinds of imprudent and reckless behaviour, because that IS what being a free thinker looks like in real time. In the modern world of social media surveillance, we have that microscope on every contemporary maverick — and we routinely use it to dismiss them. We should expect mavericks to look like rubbish in close-up; the price of demanding clean records from outlaws is having no outlaws.
core_ideas.quote: We have damaged the creative process. We have damaged the innovation process.

core_ideas.explanation: Because Vindication of the Rights of Woman could only be read by the men who read political philosophy, Wollstonecraft had to argue that women's emancipation would make them better daughters, sisters, wives, and mothers — not that women would be autonomous and not need men. The costume of the audience is the price of being heard. The first generation of any radical idea has to smuggle the radicalism through the audience's existing assumptions; the next generation can drop the costume.
core_ideas.quote: Would men but generously snap our chains and be content with rational fellowship in instead of slavish obedience, they would find us... in a word, better citizens.

core_ideas.explanation: Reading Mary Shelley's Frankenstein today, one finds cliches everywhere — but they are cliches now BECAUSE she invented them. Same with Fritz Lang's Metropolis in cinema, much of Shakespeare in language. Don't judge a pioneer for the cliches in their work; trace the cliche back to see whose work first made it a cliche.
core_ideas.quote: They weren't cliches there. They sort of originated with her work.

core_ideas.concept: Science Advances One Funeral At A Time
core_ideas.explanation: Max Planck's principle: new scientific paradigms gain acceptance not because opponents are convinced, but because they die off and are replaced by a generation that grew up with the new idea as background. Semmelweis (1865), Boltzmann (1906), Wegener (1930), Mendel (forgotten until decades later) — all illustrate. The Boltzmann timing is especially cruel: he killed himself two years before vindication.
core_ideas.quote: Science changes one funeral at a time.

core_ideas.concept: The Selection-Bias Pipeline Of Modern Knowledge
core_ideas.explanation: Lay out the modern intellectual career in steps: 11th and 12th class exams to get into college; college grades to get into PhD; lab work and three boring papers to graduate; the right walk-talk-dress to get an academic job; published papers and grants to get tenure. At every step the requirement is: keep your head down, do not challenge the establishment, do not rock the boat. The pipeline is a near-perfect filter against the very kinds of imagination that produce continental drift, statistical mechanics, mRNA vaccines, or evolution. By the time someone has the credentials to be heard, they have been selected to have nothing surprising to say.
core_ideas.quote: How do you get papers published? How do you get grants? By being one of the boys, by playing the game.

core_ideas.concept: Aggressive Conventionality Amplified By Social Media
core_ideas.explanation: The aggressively conventional-minded behaviour that wrecked Semmelweis over decades now happens on a much faster time-scale. Twitter's ideological tribes — right and left — punish dissent within their own dogmas; the aggressively conventional in those spaces are also virtue-signalling for status within the tribe, doubling the incentive to attack heretics. People get cancelled, ostracised, become outcasts in days, not years. The substance hasn't changed; the velocity has.
core_ideas.quote: Aggressively conventional-minded behavior can get amplified by social media.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: On Mary Shelley's husband editing only ~4,000 of Frankenstein's 78,000 words: 'And if you go through the book, I think you'll agree with me that those are the bad writing — they stand out.'
Amit on the typical sexist reaction to a woman writing Frankenstein: 'Oh her husband must have written it.' (And: Percy Shelley's own novels are pretty bad.)
Amit on Darwin: 'Amitbhai, you'll be pleased to know he was as great a book writer as you.' / Amit: 'He took a long time, you mean. Very long time.'

Ajay on Wallace cracking evolution in a 106-degree fever: 'Gentle reader, please hope that your creative energies are fueled by malaria... Amitbhai, you may consider getting a little malaria to assist your projects.'
Amit on Darwin's twenty-two-year delay before Wallace beat him to it: 'Some bachcha got malaria and rent it up — Mathew bhai salsa kam karo.'
Amit on Darwin being caricatured as a monkey: 'It was just — he had a face for that.'
Ajay on Newton hoarding the calculus from humanity: 'How can humans understand it? It's like — I'm Newton.'
Amit on the staircase under which Keynes had a heart attack: 'I said, wow, so did he say in the short run we are all dead?'

Amit warning Ajay before recommendations: 'Please give a conventional recommendation, because last time you said something about go to Huntsville, Arizona. So don't send me anywhere now.' Ajay: 'I said you may consider visiting Huntsville, ALABAMA.'
Ajay's recommendation of the episode is, of course, oddball anyway: visit Boltzmann's tombstone in Vienna — 'on his tombstone is written S = k log W.'
Amit on his population column: when readers cannot rebut the argument, 'gali nala gay' (the abuse-pipe gets opened).
Amit on the show being one hour with mad people: 'That's why I do this show with you.' / Ajay: 'Absolutely.'
St. Pancras churchyard, London — the gravestone of Mary Wollstonecraft on which her daughter Mary Shelley learned to write.

Thomas Taylor, A Vindication for the Rights of Brutes — a satire of Wollstonecraft's book arguing that if women have rights, animals should too. (Peter Singer's Animal Liberation would later make exactly that argument seriously.)
Horace Walpole's epithet for Mary Wollstonecraft: 'a hyena in petticoats.'
Brian Aldiss's claim that Mary Shelley's Frankenstein is the first work of science fiction.

Milton, Paradise Lost: 'Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay / To mould Me man? Did I solicit thee / From darkness to promote me?' — the lines that seeded Frankenstein's creature confronting Frankenstein.

William Lawrence — the early-19th-century anatomist whose lectures Polidori had attended, arguing there is no soul, that consciousness is merely the organs of the body. The catalyst Mary Shelley rolled into Frankenstein.

John Locke — Amit's 'intellectual hero,' banned by Cambridge in 1701; his right-to-self-ownership philosophy seeded liberal rights theory and the American Declaration of Independence ('We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal') — and was passed to Wollstonecraft via her neighbour Reverend Henry Clare.
Wollstonecraft's response-book A Vindication of the Rights of Men (1790), against Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France — written before her 1792 Vindication of the Rights of Woman.
Margaret Atwood and Ursula K. Le Guin — Amit's exemplars of science fiction as serious literature, in the lineage Mary Shelley invented.
Newton vs Leibniz on calculus — Ajay's parallel for Darwin vs Wallace: both reach the idea, the slow careful one nearly gets scooped, both end up presenting at once.
Pangaea — the single supercontinent ~260 million years ago that Wegener proposed had broken apart.
S = k log W — Boltzmann's entropy equation, inscribed on his Vienna tombstone.
John Snow's 1854 London cholera investigation that traced the disease to water — and W.C. Pernell's later cholera maps in India that incidentally indicted caste.
Katalin Kariko — vindicated mRNA pioneer; her 'grant, grant, grant... no, no, no' line stands as motto for a long career of being right and rejected.

Robert George (Princeton) and his thought experiment for history students: 'You are a white Southerner before abolition — which way do you go?' Every hand goes up for abolitionist; almost none would have.
Andrei Sakharov, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn — examples of mavericks whose 'WikiLeaks dump' would not survive modern surveillance, despite the brilliance of their public work.
The Planck Principle — 'Science changes one funeral at a time.'
Hamlet: 'All that glisters is not gold' — Ajay corrects the popular misquote 'all that glitters is not gold.'
Vikram Raghavan — World Bank lawyer and history obsessive who walked Ajay through Washington DC, pointing out the staircase under which Keynes once had a heart attack.
Tyler Cowen and Shruti Rajagopalan's Emergent Ventures — explicitly funding non-credentialed weirdos with mad ideas, as the institutional answer to the moonshot drought.
